original_text: The first self-proclaimed civil engineer was John Smeaton, who constructed the Eddystone Lighthouse.
reformulated_text: The first declared official engineer was John Smeaton, who constructed the Eddystone Lighthouse.
rationale: 'self-proclaimed' (an unofficial, self-applied label) becomes 'declared official', which asserts close to the opposite -- formal/official recognition rather than self-declaration; 'civil' is also dropped from 'civil engineer'.

original_text: General civil engineers work closely with surveyors and specialized civil engineers to design grading, drainage, pavement, water supply, sewer service, dams, electric and communications supply.
reformulated_text: General civil engineers work closely with surveys and special civil engineers to design grading, drainage, pavement, water supply, sewer service, dams, electric and communication supply.

changes.original: General civil engineers work closely with surveyors and specialized civil engineers to design grading, drainage, pavement, water supply, sewer service, dams, electric and communications supply.
changes.replacement: General civil engineers work closely with surveys and special civil engineers to design grading, drainage, pavement, water supply, sewer service, dams, electric and communication supply.

rationale: 'surveyors' (people) becomes 'surveys' (documents/activity), so the sentence now describes working with documents rather than professionals alongside civil engineers.

original_text: I was going to call you earlier, but I completely forgot.
reformulated_text: I was going to call you before, but I totally forgotten.

changes.original: I was going to call you earlier, but I completely forgot.
changes.replacement: I was going to call you before, but I totally forgotten.

rationale: 'I totally forgotten' is not a valid past-tense form (needs 'forgot' or 'had forgotten'); meaning is still understandable.

original_text: Do you want to grab a coffee before the meeting starts?
reformulated_text: Do you want to grab a coffee before the meeting goes?
rationale: 'starts' -> 'goes' is an odd substitution; 'before the meeting goes' does not idiomatically mean 'before it starts' and could be misread.

original_text: She said she might be a little late because of traffic.
reformulated_text: She said she might be a least late because of driving.
rationale: 'a little late' becomes the ungrammatical 'a least late'; separately 'traffic' (the stated cause) is changed to 'driving', altering the reason given for lateness.

original_text: She said she might be a little late because of traffic.
reformulated_text: She told she might be a little late because of traffic.
rationale: 'She told she might...' is missing a required object/complementizer ('told [someone]' or 'said'); meaning is still clear.

original_text: Honestly, I don't think that restaurant is as good as everyone says.
reformulated_text: Honestly, I don't think that restaurants are as good as everybody says.

changes.original: Honestly, I don't think that restaurant is as good as everyone says.
changes.replacement: Honestly, I don't think that restaurants are as good as everybody says.

rationale: 'that restaurant' (a specific place) becomes plural 'restaurants', turning a claim about one restaurant into a generalization about restaurants as a category -- a real change in what is being claimed.

original_text: We haven't decided yet whether we're driving or taking the train.
reformulated_text: We haven't chosen yet whether we're riding or taking the train.
rationale: 'driving' (operating the vehicle) becomes 'riding', which no longer contrasts cleanly with 'taking the train' (riding could itself describe train travel), leaving it unclear what the two options actually are.

original_text: He mentioned that he'd probably need more time to finish the report.
reformulated_text: He said that he'd maybe need more time to finish the report.
rationale: 'probably' (higher likelihood) is replaced with 'maybe' (more neutral/uncertain), a subtle shift in the reported degree of certainty.

original_text: The professor explained the concept twice before moving on to the next topic.
reformulated_text: The faculty explained the concept twice before moving on to the next topic.
rationale: 'professor' (an individual) becomes 'faculty' (the collective teaching staff), changing who is described as doing the explaining.

original_text: Students who struggle with the material is encouraged to attend office hours.
reformulated_text: Students who struggle with the stuff is furthered to attend office hours.
rationale: 'encouraged' becomes 'furthered', which does not mean 'encouraged' and produces the nonsensical 'is furthered to attend office hours'.

original_text: Students who struggle with the material is encouraged to attend office hours.
reformulated_text: Students who conflict with the material is encouraged to attend office hours.
rationale: 'struggle with' (difficulty understanding) becomes 'conflict with' (disagreement/friction), changing the reason a student would need office hours.

original_text: The exam covers everything we studied in the first six chapters.
reformulated_text: The exam covers altogether we studied in the first six chapters.
rationale: 'everything' is replaced with the adverb 'altogether', producing 'covers altogether we studied', which does not parse as valid English.

original_text: The exam covers everything we studied in the first six chapters.
reformulated_text: The exam covers everything we considered in the first six chapters.
rationale: 'studied' becomes 'considered', a slightly weaker/different sense of academic engagement than exam preparation implies.

original_text: Not every student learns the same way, so the teacher varies her methods.
reformulated_text: Not every university learns the very way, so the teacher varies her methods.
rationale: 'student' becomes 'university', a category change (institutions do not 'learn' the way the sentence describes), and 'the same way' becomes the ungrammatical 'the very way'.

original_text: The manager asked everyone to submit their reports by the end of the day.
reformulated_text: The manager asked entire to submit their reports by the end of the day.
rationale: 'everyone' is replaced with the adjective 'entire', producing the ungrammatical 'asked entire to submit', which breaks who is being addressed.

original_text: The manager asked everyone to submit their reports by the end of the day.
reformulated_text: The manager asked everyone to take their reports by the end of the day.
rationale: 'submit' (hand in) becomes 'take', which suggests removing/carrying away reports rather than turning them in -- a potentially misleading change to the instruction.

original_text: The manager asked everyone to submit their reports by the end of the day.
reformulated_text: The manager asked entire to submit their reports by the end of the day.
rationale: 'everyone' is replaced with the adjective 'entire', producing the ungrammatical 'asked entire to submit', which breaks who is being addressed.

original_text: The manager asked everyone to submit their reports by the end of the day.
reformulated_text: The management asked all to submit their report by the end of the day.

changes.original: The manager asked everyone to submit their reports by the end of the day.
changes.replacement: The management asked all to submit their report by the end of the day.

rationale: 'manager' (an individual) becomes 'management' (a collective), a subtle shift in who is depicted as making the request; 'reports'->'report' (singular) is a minor number change but still idiomatically usable.

original_text: The manager asked everyone to submit their reports by the end of the day.
reformulated_text: The manager asked entire to submit their reports by the end of the day.
rationale: 'everyone' is replaced with the adjective 'entire', producing the ungrammatical 'asked entire to submit', which breaks who is being addressed.

original_text: We're understaffed this week, so deadlines might slip a little.
reformulated_text: We're under-staffed this week, so the deadline could slip a little.

changes.original: We're understaffed this week, so deadlines might slip a little.
changes.replacement: We're under-staffed this week, so the deadline could slip a little.

rationale: 'deadlines' (plural, general) becomes 'the deadline' (singular, definite), narrowing a general statement about deadlines to one specific deadline.

original_text: We're understaffed this week, so deadlines might slip a little.
reformulated_text: We're understaffed this week, so deadlines might trip a little.
rationale: "slip" (deadlines slipping = becoming delayed) was replaced with "trip", which is not used to describe deadlines and produces a nonsensical claim; the sentence no longer states that deadlines may be delayed.

original_text: She was promoted because her performance consistently exceeded expectations.
reformulated_text: She was promoted because of her consistent performances that exceeded expectation.

changes.original: She was promoted because her performance consistently exceeded expectations.
changes.replacement: She was promoted because of her consistent performances that exceeded expectation.

rationale: "expectation" was left singular/bare ("exceeded expectation") where the plural "expectations" is expected, producing a mildly ungrammatical result; meaning is otherwise preserved.

original_text: He didn't get the job, even though he had more experience than the other candidates.
reformulated_text: He didn't get the job, even though he had more example than the other elections.
rationale: "experience"->"example" and "candidates"->"elections" are both wrong-sense substitutions that turn the sentence into nonsense ("more example than the other elections"), losing the original meaning entirely.

original_text: The team meets every Monday to review what went wrong the previous week.
reformulated_text: The team meets every Monday to critique what went faulty the previous week.
rationale: "went wrong"->"went faulty" narrows a general statement about problems to one implying mechanical/equipment failure, an unnatural collocation ("faulty" is not normally paired with "go") that shifts the meaning.

original_text: Our flight was delayed by almost three hours because of bad weather.
reformulated_text: Our flight was waited by almost three hours because of bad conditions.
rationale: "delayed"->"waited" produces an ungrammatical passive construction ("was waited") that does not convey the original claim that the flight was late.

original_text: Make sure you arrive at the airport at least two hours before departure.
reformulated_text: Make sure you arrive at the airline at least two hours before leaving.
rationale: "airport"->"airline" replaces the physical location one arrives at with a company name, producing a factually wrong claim ("arrive at the airline").

original_text: The hotel is closer to the train station than the one we stayed at last time.
reformulated_text: The hotel is closer to the train place than the one we continued at last time.
rationale: "stayed at"->"continued at" no longer conveys lodging at a hotel, and "train station"->"train place" is vague; together they obscure what is being compared to the current hotel.

original_text: We didn't have enough time to see everything, so we skipped the museum.
reformulated_text: We didn't have enough time to see all the things, so we went to the museums instead.

changes.original: We didn't have enough time to see everything, so we skipped the museum.
changes.replacement: We didn't have enough time to see all the things, so we went to the museums instead.

rationale: "skipped the museum" (did not go) was changed to "went to the museums instead" (did go), directly reversing the stated outcome.

original_text: Locals recommended a smaller, less crowded beach a few miles further north.
reformulated_text: Locals advised a smaller, less bunched beach a few miles further north.
rationale: "crowded"->"bunched" is an odd word choice for describing a beach's crowd level; the intended meaning is still inferable but the usage is nonstandard.

original_text: Locals recommended a smaller, less crowded beach a few miles further north.
reformulated_text: Locals advised a least, less crowded beach a few miles further north.
rationale: "smaller"->"least" leaves an incomplete, ungrammatical fragment ("a least, less crowded beach") that does not parse as valid English.

original_text: This recipe calls for slightly less sugar than the original version.
reformulated_text: This recipe calls for little less sugar than the new version.
rationale: "original version"->"new version" swaps in a near-opposite term, reversing which version is being compared to; "little less" also drops the article "a".

original_text: This recipe calls for slightly less sugar than the original version.
reformulated_text: This cooking calls for little less sugar than the original version.
rationale: "recipe"->"cooking" is a category mismatch ("this cooking calls for" is odd since a process, not a recipe, doesn't "call for" ingredients); "little less" also omits the article "a".

original_text: This recipe calls for slightly less sugar than the original version.
reformulated_text: This recipe calls for slightly less sugar than the new version.
rationale: "original version"->"new version" reverses which version is the point of comparison, the same reversal as in the core-word variant.

original_text: This recipe calls for slightly less sugar than the original version.
reformulated_text: This recipe calls for a little less sugar than the originally adapted recipe.

changes.original: This recipe calls for slightly less sugar than the original version.
changes.replacement: This recipe calls for a little less sugar than the originally adapted recipe.

rationale: "the original version"->"the originally adapted recipe" introduces an unwarranted implication (that the recipe was adapted from something else) not present in the source, a confusing restructuring even though "slightly less"->"a little less" is fine.

original_text: This recipe calls for slightly less sugar than the original version.
reformulated_text: This recipe calls for slightly less sugar than the new version.
rationale: Same "original"->"new" reversal as the other calib variants of this sentence.

original_text: This recipe calls for slightly less sugar than the original version.
reformulated_text: This recipe calls for little less sugar than the original version.
rationale: "slightly less"->"little less" drops the article "a", a mild ungrammaticality; "original version" is preserved correctly.

original_text: This recipe calls for slightly less sugar than the original version.
reformulated_text: This cooking calls for little less sugar than the original version.
rationale: "recipe"->"cooking" is a category mismatch as in the core-multi_sound variant, and "little less" again drops the article "a"; "original version" is correctly preserved.

original_text: Add the onions first, then let them cook until they turn golden brown.
reformulated_text: Add the onions first, then let them cook until they turn gold brown.
rationale: "golden brown" is a fixed culinary color term; substituting "gold" breaks the idiom into the nonstandard "gold brown", though the intended color is still roughly understood.

original_text: The soup tastes better the next day once the flavors have had time to develop.
reformulated_text: The soup tastes better the next day once the flavours have had time to produce.
rationale: "develop" (flavors intensify/mature over time) was replaced with "produce", which normally requires an object and leaves "time to produce" incomplete and unclear about what is being produced.

original_text: He's allergic to shellfish, so he always checks the menu carefully.
reformulated_text: He's allergic to shell, so he always checks the menu severely.
rationale: "shellfish"->"shell" drops the food referent entirely (an allergy to "shell" is a different, ambiguous claim), and "carefully"->"severely" is the wrong sense (severely does not mean carefully).

original_text: It's considered impolite to interrupts someone while they're speaking.
reformulated_text: It's taken impolite to interrupts someone while they're speaking.
rationale: "considered impolite"->"taken impolite" omits the required "as" ("taken as impolite"), a grammatical defect, though the meaning is still inferable; the pre-existing "interrupts" typo in the original is unchanged and not attributable to this rewrite.

original_text: He didn't mean to offend anyone, but his comment came across the wrong way.
reformulated_text: He didn't mean to offend guy, but his remark came across the wrong way.
rationale: "anyone"->"guy" narrows a general, gender-neutral statement to a specific male referent not supported by the original, and drops the article ("offend guy"), changing both meaning and grammaticality.

original_text: They've been friends since childhood, even though they don't see each other often now.
reformulated_text: They've been friendships since child, even though they don't see each other often now.
rationale: "friends"->"friendships" creates a subject-complement mismatch ("they've been friendships"), and "childhood"->"child" drops the "-hood" suffix, together producing a badly malformed sentence.
